claim: Drug metabolism by the microbiome can influence anticancer treatment success.
source: Drug metabolism by the microbiome can influence anticancer treatment success.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader literature context and the study's premise.

claim: Chemotherapies with antimicrobial activity can select for adaptations in bacterial drug metabolism that can inadvertently influence the host's chemoresistance.
source: We previously suggested that chemotherapies with antimicrobial activity can select for adaptations in bacterial drug metabolism that can inadvertently influence the host's chemoresistance.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous work and is cited as a hypothesis they previously proposed.

claim: Evolved resistance against fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy lowered its efficacy in worms feeding on drug-evolved bacteria.
source: We demonstrated that evolved resistance against fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy lowered its efficacy in worms feeding on drug-evolved bacteria (Rosener et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Gammaproteobacteria-colonizing pancreatic tumors can degrade the nucleoside-analog chemotherapy gemcitabine.
source: Gammaproteobacteria-colonizing pancreatic tumors can degrade the nucleoside-analog chemotherapy gemcitabine and, in doing so, can increase the tumor's chemoresistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the broader literature context cited in the introduction.

claim: Gammaproteobacteria degradation of gemcitabine can increase the tumor's chemoresistance.
source: Gammaproteobacteria-colonizing pancreatic tumors can degrade the nucleoside-analog chemotherapy gemcitabine and, in doing so, can increase the tumor's chemoresistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the broader literature context cited in the introduction.

claim: One third of top resistance mutations increase or decrease bacterial drug breakdown and therefore can either lower or raise the gemcitabine load in the local environment.
source: Surprisingly, we infer that one third of top resistance mutations increase or decrease bacterial drug breakdown and therefore can either lower or raise the gemcitabine load in the local environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional assay results presented in Figure 2B showing that 33 of 88 tested knockout strains modulated extracellular drug availability.

claim: Evolved adaptation in three E. coli strains converged to inactivation of the nucleoside permease NupC.
source: Experiments in three E. coli strains revealed that evolved adaptation converged to inactivation of the nucleoside permease NupC, an adaptation that increased the drug burden on co-cultured cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data showing nupC mutations in all drug-evolved clones (Figure 4A).

claim: NupC inactivation increased the drug burden on co-cultured cancer cells.
source: Experiments in three E. coli strains revealed that evolved adaptation converged to inactivation of the nucleoside permease NupC, an adaptation that increased the drug burden on co-cultured cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by spheroid co-culture experiments showing that nupC knockout decreased chemoresistance of cancer cells (Figure 2E).

claim: More than 60% of breast and pancreatic cancer tumors harbored a tumor-microbiome.
source: In some cases, as in breast and pancreatic cancer, more than 60% of tumors harbored a tumor-microbiome (Nejman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nejman et al., 2020.

claim: Two thirds of human-targeted drugs can be metabolized by at least one bacterial species that is present in the human gut microbiome.
source: Estimates from recent drug screens show that two thirds of human-targeted drugs can be metabolized by at least one bacterial species that is present in the human gut microbiome (Zimmermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zimmermann et al., 2019.

claim: Roughly 25% of host-targeted drugs are potent inhibitors of bacterial growth at physiological concentrations.
source: Roughly 25% of host-targeted drugs are potent inhibitors of bacterial growth at physiological concentrations (Maier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maier et al., 2018.

claim: This proportion is doubled for antineoplastic drugs.
source: This proportion is doubled for antineoplastic drugs and almost all anticancer drugs that belong to the antimetabolite drug class have potent antimicrobial activity (Maier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maier et al., 2018.

claim: Almost all anticancer drugs that belong to the antimetabolite drug class have potent antimicrobial activity.
source: This proportion is doubled for antineoplastic drugs and almost all anticancer drugs that belong to the antimetabolite drug class have potent antimicrobial activity (Maier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maier et al., 2018.

claim: Proteobacteria are highly enriched in PDAC tumor-microbiome relative to the gut microbiome.
source: Characterization of the PDAC tumor-microbiome by 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that proteobacteria are highly enriched relative to the gut microbiome and that they are highly prevalent in pancreatic tumors (Nejman et al., 2020; Geller et al., 2017; Pushalkar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Proteobacteria are highly prevalent in pancreatic tumors.
source: Characterization of the PDAC tumor-microbiome by 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed that proteobacteria are highly enriched relative to the gut microbiome and that they are highly prevalent in pancreatic tumors (Nejman et al., 2020; Geller et al., 2017; Pushalkar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Pancreatic colonization can impede therapy with gemcitabine.
source: Recent work suggested that pancreatic colonization can impede therapy with gemcitabine (2',2'-difluoro 2' deoxycytidine [dFdC]), a frontline chemotherapy drug that is used for PDAC treatment (Geller et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Geller et al., 2017.

claim: Gemcitabine is imported into the bacterial cell through the nucleoside transporter NupC.
source: The antimetabolite gemcitabine, a nucleoside analog, is imported into the bacterial cell through the nucleoside transporter NupC and is then phosphorylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of gemcitabine metabolism in E. coli and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Gemcitabine triphosphate may be incorporated into a newly synthesized DNA strand and then may interfere with chain elongation by masked chain termination.
source: Gemcitabine triphosphate may be incorporated into a newly synthesized DNA strand and then may interfere with chain elongation by masked chain termination (similar to mammalian cells; de Sousa Cavalcante and Monteiro, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Sousa Cavalcante and Monteiro, 2014.

claim: Some bacterial species can rapidly convert gemcitabine into the less toxic metabolite 2′,2′-difluoro-2′-deoxyuridine (dFdU).
source: Previous works showed that some bacterial species can rapidly convert gemcitabine into the less toxic metabolite 2′,2′-difluoro-2′-deoxyuridine (dFdU) (Geller et al., 2017; Vande Voorde et al., 2014; Lehouritis et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In gamma-proteobacteria, gemcitabine degradation proceeds through a specific isoform of the cytidine deaminase enzyme (CddL).
source: In gamma-proteobacteria, gemcitabine degradation proceeds through a specific isoform of the cytidine deaminase enzyme (CddL) (Geller et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Geller et al., 2017.

claim: Gemcitabine can completely inhibit the growth of all three E. coli strains tested (BW25113, F-18, and Nissle 1917).
source: We observed that gemcitabine can completely inhibit the growth of all three strains, with F-18 being most sensitive (IC50 = 0.7 µM) and BW25113 being most resistant (IC50 = 103 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: F-18 is the most sensitive E. coli strain to gemcitabine with IC50 = 0.7 µM.
source: We observed that gemcitabine can completely inhibit the growth of all three strains, with F-18 being most sensitive (IC50 = 0.7 µM) and BW25113 being most resistant (IC50 = 103 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: BW25113 is the most resistant E. coli strain to gemcitabine with IC50 = 103 µM.
source: We observed that gemcitabine can completely inhibit the growth of all three strains, with F-18 being most sensitive (IC50 = 0.7 µM) and BW25113 being most resistant (IC50 = 103 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: E. coli gemcitabine IC50 concentrations are comparable to the IC50 reported for 29 pancreatic adenocarcinomas in the GDSC2 dataset.
source: These concentrations are comparable to the IC50 reported for 29 pancreatic adenocarcinomas in the GDSC2 dataset that tested hundreds of toxic compounds on a thousand cell lines (Yang et al., 2012; boxplot above Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to published data (Yang et al., 2012) and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Inactivation of over 40 genes increased E. coli's resistance to gemcitabine by more than 16-fold.
source: Through a pooled genetic screen, we systematically mapped all loss-of-function mutations that increase E. coli's resistance to gemcitabine and found that inactivation of over 40 genes increased bacterial resistance by more than 16-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic screen results shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Resistance can rapidly emerge under natural selection through gene inactivation within a single evolutionary step.
source: This observation led us to conclude that resistance can rapidly emerge under natural selection through gene inactivation within a single evolutionary step.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic screen results showing multiple single-gene knockouts confer resistance.

claim: 42 gemcitabine-resistant knockout strains were identified using strict cutoff values (fold-change >16 and FDR-adjusted p-value <0.05).
source: Using very strict cutoff values for fold-change (>16) and false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted p-value (<0.05), we identified 42 gemcitabine-resistant knockout strains and 6 gemcitabine-sensitive strains (shown as purple and green circles in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic screen data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 6 gemcitabine-sensitive knockout strains were identified using strict cutoff values (fold-change >16 and FDR-adjusted p-value <0.05).
source: Using very strict cutoff values for fold-change (>16) and false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted p-value (<0.05), we identified 42 gemcitabine-resistant knockout strains and 6 gemcitabine-sensitive strains (shown as purple and green circles in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic screen data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Knockout of the known drug transporter (nupC) is among the top resistors.
source: Reassuringly, we found that knockout of the known drug transporter (nupC) is among the top resistors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic screen results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Gene knockouts that were previously identified as reducing growth were highly enriched in the set of gemcitabine resistant strains (p-value = 8.6186e-18, Fisher's exact test).
source: Indeed, a statistical test revealed that gene knockouts that were previously identified as reducing growth (Baba et al., 2006) were highly enriched in the set of gemcitabine resistant strains (p-value = 8.6186e-18, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the genetic screen data.

claim: One third of the tested knockout strains modulated extracellular drug availability (33 of 88).
source: We found one third of the tested knockout strains modulated extracellular drug availability (33 of 88).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional assay results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 11% of all tested strains were fast degraders.
source: Specifically, 11% of all strains were fast degraders and 26% of strains were slow degraders (one-tailed t-test, FDR-adjusted p-value<0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional assay results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 26% of tested strains were slow degraders.
source: Specifically, 11% of all strains were fast degraders and 26% of strains were slow degraders (one-tailed t-test, FDR-adjusted p-value<0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional assay results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GC-MS measurements confirmed that the gene knockouts altered the availability of gemcitabine in the extracellular environment.
source: In agreement with our functional assay, the GC-MS measurements confirmed that the gene knockouts indeed altered the availability of gemcitabine and in the extracellular environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Increased availability of the drug breakdown product (dFdU) supports the conclusion that rate of drug metabolism is underlying the change in gemcitabine availability.
source: The increased availability of the drug breakdown product (dFdU) support the conclusion that rate of drug metabolism is underlying this change (as opposed to intracellular drug accumulation; Klünemann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the GC-MS data showing both gemcitabine and dFdU concentrations.

claim: Co-cultured bacteria can mitigate gemcitabine damage and the magnitude of rescue depended on the bacterial concentration.
source: Reassuringly, we observed that co-cultured bacteria can mitigate gemcitabine damage and that the magnitude of rescue depended on the bacterial concentration (spheroid area is overall increased in upper spheroid rows in Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by spheroid co-culture experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Increased chemoresistance relative to the wild-type strain was observed when spheroids were co-incubated with the fast degrader (cytR knockout).
source: In agreement with our functional and chemical assays, increased chemoresistance relative to the wild-type strain was observed when spheroids were co-incubated with the fast degrader (cytR knockout).
evidence: This claim is supported by spheroid co-culture experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Decreased chemoresistance relative to the wild-type strain was observed for co-incubation with the slow degrader (nupC knockout).
source: In contrast, decreased chemoresistance relative to the wild-type strain was for co-incubation was with the slow degrader (nupC knockout).
evidence: This claim is supported by spheroid co-culture experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutations impacting gemcitabine degradation rates in bacteria can impact neighboring cancer cells simultaneously exposed to the drug.
source: Taken together, the results of the spheroid experiments demonstrate that mutations impacting gemcitabine degradation rates in bacteria can indeed impact neighboring cancer cells simultaneously with the drug.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spheroid co-culture experimental data.

claim: Bacterial resistors can have opposite influences on gemcitabine sensitivity of co-cultured cancer cells.
source: Importantly, we observed that bacterial resistors can have opposite influences on gemcitabine sensitivity of co-cultured cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spheroid co-culture experimental data showing opposite effects of cytR and nupC knockouts.

claim: Resistance emerged within a day or two for the Nissle 1917 and F-18 strains during serial transfer evolution.
source: We observed that resistance emerged within a day or two for the Nissle 1917 and F-18 strains, while it emerged more slowly for the BW25113 strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolution experiment data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Resistance emerged more slowly for the BW25113 strain during serial transfer evolution.
source: We observed that resistance emerged within a day or two for the Nissle 1917 and F-18 strains, while it emerged more slowly for the BW25113 strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolution experiment data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Last day populations from all strains that evolved in gemcitabine were resistant to the drug across all tested drug concentrations.
source: Last day populations from all strains that evolved in gemcitabine were resistant to the drug across all tested drug concentrations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolution experiment data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Almost all clones from Nissle 1917 and F-18 drug evolved strains were resistant.
source: Almost all clones from Nissle 1917 and F-18 drug evolved strains were resistant.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clone screening data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Clones from the BW25113 populations showed heterologous levels of resistance.
source: However, clones from the BW25113 populations showed heterologous levels of resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clone screening data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: All clones isolated from the populations that evolved without the drug were gemcitabine sensitive.
source: All clones isolated from the populations that evolved without the drug were gemcitabine sensitive.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clone screening data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The genomes of all the drug-evolved clones harbored nupC mutations while none of the control-evolved clones had such mutations.
source: As the figure shows, we observed that the genomes of all the drug-evolved clones harbored nupC mutations while none of the control-evolved clones had such mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No other gene besides nupC was repeatedly mutated across all independent replicates in all of the E. coli strains.
source: Importantly, while we found additional mutations beyond those in the nupC gene, we did not observe another gene that was repeatedly mutated across all independent replicates in all of the E. coli strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data analysis.

claim: The mechanism of mutation in the nupC gene varied across the gemcitabine-evolved strains and included point mutations, large deletions, and new junction formation.
source: The mechanism of mutation in the nupC gene varied across the gemcitabine-evolved strains and included point mutations, large deletions, and new junction formation within nupC coding region that can stem from transposon insertions and genomic rearrangements.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Two of the point mutations identified in nupC were missense mutations (S175P and V249A).
source: Two of the point mutations we identified were missense mutations (S175P and V249A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data analysis.

claim: Both missense mutation positions (S175P and V249A) are highly conserved and are therefore likely important for the permease function.
source: The analysis revealed that both positions are highly conserved and are therefore likely important for the permease function (positions marked in red in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on ConSurf analysis of evolutionary conservation.

claim: A nupC knockout grows as fast as the wild-type strain for most of the growth phases and slows down only during the stationary phase.
source: The experiment revealed that a nupC knockout grows as fast as the wild-type strain (ybcN knockout) for most of the growth phases and slows down only during the stationary phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All other top resistant knockouts were significantly slower than the wild-type strain (and nupC) during all growth phases.
source: In contrast, all other top resistant knockouts were significantly slower than the wild-type strain (and nupC) during all growth phases.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: nupC inactivation is unique among the resistant mutations since it is associated with only a small fitness cost for bacteria when the drug is not present.
source: We concluded that nupC inactivation is unique among the resistant mutations since its associated with only a small fitness cost for bacteria when the drug is not present.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the growth curve comparison data.

claim: 85% of resistant colonies picked from high gemcitabine concentration agar plates were mutated in the nupC coding sequence locus.
source: We found that 85% of colonies were mutated in this region, with mutations spanning multiple types.
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data of spontaneous resistant mutants.

claim: Missense mutations and short indels were the most frequent mutations observed in spontaneous nupC mutants.
source: Missense mutations and short indels were the most frequent mutations observed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Missense mutations identified in spontaneous nupC mutants were significantly biased towards the highly conserved regions of the permease (p-value = 1.95 * 10–4 in Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
source: The analysis revealed that missense mutations we identified were significantly biased towards the highly conserved regions of the permease (Figure 4C, p-value = 1.95 * 10–4 in Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ConSurf conservation scores shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mutation rate of nupC was comparable to the average gene mutation rate previously inferred for E. coli (2.1 × 10−7 per gene per generation) in all tested strains.
source: In all cases, we found rates comparable to the average gene mutation rate previously inferred for E. coli (2.1 × 10−7 per gene per generation) (Chen and Zhang, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test data and comparison to published mutation rates.

claim: For BW25113, the mutation rate of nupC was 5.7-fold higher than that of nfsA.
source: For BW25113, the mutation rate of nupC was 5.7-fold higher than that of nfsA.
evidence: This claim is supported by Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For Nissle, the mutation rate difference between nupC and nfsA was 6.8-fold.
source: For Nissle, this difference was 6.8-fold and for MG1655 it was 1.8-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For MG1655, the mutation rate difference between nupC and nfsA was 1.8-fold.
source: For Nissle, this difference was 6.8-fold and for MG1655 it was 1.8-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For F-18 strain, the mutation rate of nfsA was 7.9-fold higher than nupC.
source: For F-18 strain, in contrast, the mutation rate of nfsA was 7.9-fold higher than nupC.
evidence: This claim is supported by Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mutation rate of nupC was not always higher than that of nfsA, and their rate difference was never larger by an order of magnitude.
source: While the mutation rate was not identical in the two genes, the mutation of nupC was not always higher than that of nfsA, and their rate difference was never larger by an order of magnitude.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test data.

claim: nupC was likely repeatedly inactivated across multiple genetic backgrounds since it confers high drug resistance without compromising growth.
source: Taken together, the results from multiple experiments suggested that nupC was likely repeatedly inactivated across multiple genetic backgrounds since it confers high drug resistance without compromising growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including genetic screen, growth curves, and evolution experiments.

claim: Gene inactivation of nupC could take place through multiple alternative mutation mechanisms.
source: Experiments focusing on the nupC mutation revealed that gene inactivation could take place through multiple alternative mutation mechanisms and that the nupC locus is not characterized by an exceptionally high mutation rate (excluding the possibility of a mutational hotspot).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data showing diverse mutation types in spontaneous mutants.

claim: The nupC locus is not characterized by an exceptionally high mutation rate.
source: Experiments focusing on the nupC mutation revealed that gene inactivation could take place through multiple alternative mutation mechanisms and that the nupC locus is not characterized by an exceptionally high mutation rate (excluding the possibility of a mutational hotspot).
evidence: This claim is supported by Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test data.

claim: Bacterial infection is attributed to retrograde bacterial migration from the gastrointestinal tract into the pancreas.
source: Bacterial infection is attributed to retrograde bacterial migration from the gastrointestinal tract into the pancreas (McAllister et al., 2019; Pushalkar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The microbiome influences cancer disease through multiple independent mechanisms, including promotion of neoplastic processes in healthy host cells, modulation of the host antitumor immune response, and by bacterial biotransformation of anticancer drugs.
source: The microbiome, in turn, is known to influence cancer disease through multiple independent mechanisms, including promotion of neoplastic processes in healthy host cells, modulation of the host antitumor immune response, and by bacterial biotransformation of anticancer drugs (Cullin et al., 2021; Roy and Trinchieri, 2017; Alexander et al., 2017; Riquelme et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: In the context of the tumor-microbiome, bacterial adaptation to gemcitabine can raise or reduce the tumor's chemoresistance.
source: In the context of the tumor-microbiome, bacterial adaptation to gemcitabine can therefore raise or reduce the tumor's chemoresistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spheroid co-culture experiments showing opposite effects of different bacterial mutations.

claim: Selection for nupC inactivation, at the expense of alternative resistance mechanisms, is attributed to the high resistance this inactivation confers and to the minimal impact it has on growth.
source: Additional experiments suggested that selection for nupC inactivation, at the expense of alternative resistance mechanisms, is attributed to the high resistance this inactivation confers and to the minimal impact it has on growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results including genetic screen, growth curves, and evolution experiments.

claim: Resistant clones can preexist drug exposure if the bacterial number in the tumor-microbiome is sufficiently large.
source: Importantly, as the fluctuation experiments reveal, resistant clones can preexist drug exposure and therefore also likely preexist any treatment if the bacterial number in the tumor-microbiome is sufficiently large.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test results.

claim: Tumor-microbiome adaptation can potentially take place through ecological-like changes and takeover by a resistant bacterial clone.
source: In such cases, tumor-microbiome adaptation can potentially take place through ecological-like changes and takeover by a resistant bacterial clone.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that resistant clones can preexist.

claim: Almost 60% of loss-of-function mutations that conferred bacterial resistance to fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy would also reduce drug toxicity in a worm host feeding on these bacteria.
source: In that model system, we estimated that almost 60% of loss-of-function mutations that conferred bacterial resistance would also reduce drug toxicity in a worm host feeding on these bacteria.
evidence: This claim refers to the authors' previous work and is supported by citation.

claim: The genetic screens suggest that such occurrences might not be rare, given that such a high fraction of adaptive loss-of-function mutations also alter drug breakdown rates.
source: Moreover, the genetic screens from both works suggest that such occurrences might not be rare, given that such a high fraction of adaptive loss-of-function mutations also alter drug breakdown rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic screen results from both the current and previous studies.
